title: NSIC Rc 766 (Salinas 40) Rice Variety: Characteristics and Grain Quality
metaTitle: NSIC Rc 766 Rice Variety: Characteristics and Grain Quality
metaDescription: NSIC Rc 766 is an inbred rice for saline prone fields, approved in 2024. See its pest and disease ratings, grain quality and where it grows best.
excerpt: NSIC Rc 766 is an inbred rice variety for saline prone fields, known locally as Salinas 40. The NSIC approved it in 2024. PhilRice bred it. PhilRice has not listed its days to harvest and trial yield yet, but its pest ratings and grain quality are below.

heroImage.alt: Farmers transplanting rice, as on the saline prone fields NSIC Rc 766 is bred for

blocks.text: If you came here looking for rice variety 766, or Rc 766, this is the one. The facts below come from sources that include PhilRice and its public seed database. So you can compare it with the other varieties in our [rice variety finder](/rice-varieties) before you buy seed. Also read our guide to [rice varieties in the Philippines](/crops/rice-varieties-philippines) for how inbreds, hybrids and special rice differ.

items: **Watch out for:** rice blast, tungro, sheath blight.
**Cooked rice:** intermediate amylose, so soft but not sticky.

blocks.text: How many days does it take, and how much does it yield?

PhilRice has not published this variety's days to harvest and trial yields in its catalogue yet. So ask the seed seller or your municipal agriculturist for the figures from the trials in your region before you plan the season. Once you know the day count, anee.io dates every task from each lot's own planting day, with the [growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside it. Meanwhile, our guide to [raising rice yield per hectare](/blog/increase-rice-yield-per-hectare) covers the habits that matter with any variety.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?

blocks.caption: Reactions in PhilRice's tests: R resistant, MR moderately resistant, I intermediate, MS moderately susceptible, S susceptible. Some carry a second rating in brackets, as PhilRice lists them.
rows: Took a middling share of damage

blocks.text: So scout early for [rice blast](/diseases/rice-blast), [tungro](/diseases/rice-tungro), [sheath blight](/diseases/sheath-blight). When you see the first signs, check the guide before you spray, because the right timing saves more than an extra dose. If you are not sure what you see, our [pest and disease finders](/features/pest-and-disease-finders) help you name it from the damage.

blocks.caption: Grain quality in PhilRice's seed database

blocks.text: Amylose decides how rice cooks. With intermediate amylose, expect rice that is soft but not sticky. In fact, PhilRice notes that Filipino taste moved from high to intermediate and low amylose rice, because people want it softer. Head rice is the share of whole grains after milling. So a higher number means fewer broken grains and a better price at the mill.

It suits fields where salt reaches the soil, such as coastal paddies. So flush the field with fresh water before planting when you can. Our guide to [saline soil preparation](/land-preparation/saline-soil-preparation) shows what helps. For the right month in your province, see [the best time to plant rice](/blog/best-time-to-plant-rice-philippines).

items.q: What is the local name of NSIC Rc 766?
items.a: It is known as Salinas 40. Seed sellers and agriculturists use both names, so ask for either one.
The NSIC approved it in 2024. PhilRice bred it. PhilRice has not listed its days to harvest and trial yield yet, so ask for the regional trial figures before you plant.
No, it is an inbred. So the seed you buy grows true, but certified seed still gives the best start, as PalayCheck advises.

items.q: What should I watch for when I plant it?
items.a: In PhilRice's tests it was weak against rice blast, tungro, sheath blight. So scout from the early weeks and act at the first signs.
It has intermediate amylose, 20 percent. So it cooks soft but not sticky.

items.q: Where can I buy certified seed of this variety?
items.a: Ask accredited seed growers in your province, your municipal agriculturist or the nearest PhilRice station. Look for the certified seed tag on the sack before you pay.
